title: Pepper spray was used by police
article: Police pepper-sprayed Michael Stochmal just minutes before the 35- year-old man, who'd just stabbed his young son to death, died of an apparent heart attack.
It's the second time this summer a suspect died after being pepper-sprayed by Regina police.
However Regina Police Chief Cal Johnston cautioned against connecting the use of pepper spray and the deaths.
"To just leap to a conclusion that pepper spray is a casual fact is not appropriate," Johnston said.
The most recent death happened Saturday night after police were called to a home at 6 Plentywood Bay in North Regina where they found the body of nine-year-old Justin Stochmal.
The boy's father, Michael, was shouting, appeared delusional and drunk and was trying to take his clothes off. He had just killed his son.
While eight police officers attempted to subdue Stochmal, Johnston said it became necessary to use pepper spray. Shortly after, Stochmal died of an apparent heart attack.

"I was worried they might have used spray," said Bob Hughes, spokesman for the Saskatchewan Coalition Against Racism (SCAR). Hughes is not the same Bob Hughes who is executive editor of The Leader-Post.

"We believe when people are experiencing mental health episodes that pepper spray shouldn't be used," Hughes said, adding it causes respiratory problems and can exacerbate existing medical conditions.
The use of pepper spray became a subject of debate in July when 32-year-old Vernon Crowe died.
Police used pepper spray to subdue Crowe, while the man was being transported to hospital after an apparent epileptic seizure.
Police say Crowe had become agitated and combative in the ambulance.
While Johnston reiterated the lack of evidence connecting pepper spray to the deaths, he said Crowe's death prompted police to search for how the man may have died.
That search led to a condition known as "excited delirium." Johnston said the condition is marked by prolonged periods of extreme emotional and physical exertion.
It's also often connected with confrontations with police and can lead to heart failure, Johnston said.
Toxicology results are still incomplete for both Stochmal and Crowe.

And Johnston said in compliance with usual procedure for police- related death, the major crimes unit will investigate Stochmal's death. Any findings will be turned over to Saskatchewan Justice and to the coroner.
Funerals for Stochmal and his son will be held Friday.
